items.heading: Copycat does not always win
items.text: "Copycat wins" holds only under some noise levels and payoffs. The game teaches the conditions, never a champion.

sources.label: The Evolution of Trust, full text

items.heading: Bid figures show a link, not a cause
items.text: Gottman's bid figures (86% and 33%) come from observation and show correlation. The game never shows a bid score as a health score for real relationships.

sources.label: Simply Psychology on the limits of the bid research

items.heading: Real cities sort less than the model
items.text: Schelling-style models predict more sorting than real cities show, and real segregation also has institutional and economic causes. The Lily Shallows margin notes say so.

sources.label: Understanding the Social Context of the Schelling Segregation Model, Clark and Fossett, 2008
The Color of Law, Richard Rothstein, 2017

items.heading: The friendship claim is contested
items.text: The claim that close friendships fell sharply from 1985 to 2004 is contested. The game does not use it.

items.heading: What the model leaves out
items.text: Each creature here is a handful of numbers and a few rules. The model leaves out words, bodies, money, power, and history, and every other reason a real person shares or keeps. It gives each tie one number for warmth on each side, and each creature the same kind of memory. Use it to ask questions about trust. Do not use it to answer them about real people.

sources.label: The Evolution of Trust, Nicky Case
